name: presentational-vs-container
intent: Separate what a component looks like from where its data comes from: presentational components render the values and callbacks handed to them and know nothing about the application, while the supply half - a container component, hook, state holder or template-rendering view - owns the data source, the loading and the behaviour.
problem: One component both decides how the screen looks and knows how to obtain its data. The markup then cannot be reused with another source, cannot be rendered in a test, story or design harness without a store or network stub, and every screen that needs the same widget forks it. The recurring decision is where to draw the line between the render half (input in, markup out) and the supply half (data access, side effects, error handling) so that the first becomes reusable and the second stays replaceable.
context: Component-based UI codebases in declarative frameworks - web (React, Vue, Angular, Blazor), mobile and desktop (Compose, SwiftUI, Qt, JavaFX) - and their server-rendered cousins (Rails partials, Django templates, Go templates), where one piece of markup must render from several data sources (live store, API payload, fixture), where design and data work are owned by different people, or where component and visual-regression tests must run without a backend. It applies as long as the markup carries no data-source dependency of its own; the shape of the supply half varies by ecosystem (wrapper component, custom hook, state holder, template action).
benefits: Presentation becomes reusable: the same presentational component renders under any source - live store, server payload, fixture - because its input contract is the only thing it depends on.
Tests and design harnesses need no backend: a presentational component renders from a literal props object, so unit, story and visual-regression tests run without a store, network or database.
Design and data work parallelise: markup, styling and accessibility evolve without touching data access, and the supply half evolves without touching markup.
The data source becomes replaceable: moving from a store to a query library, or from an API to a cache, changes the supply half only.
Failure handling is centralised: loading, retry, error and empty states live once per screen instead of being smeared across widgets that cannot know about them.
Non-domain contributors can work on the UI: because presentational components fetch nothing and mutate nothing they were given, a designer or a newcomer can change them safely.
tradeoffs: One extra component and one extra file per screen: the pattern costs a layer that a single component with a hook would not need, which is why the original article's 2019 update no longer recommends splitting components by default.
The boundary is a convention, not a compiler check: children still import the store, or containers quietly render markup, and the split decays without naming rules, lint enforcement and review.

Containers can only pass values down, so deep trees either forward props through components that ignore them or force a second channel (context, slots, dependency injection) - the very forwarding the pattern was meant to remove.
Generated containers stack: higher-order-component wrappers nest providers and make prop provenance and typing harder to follow.
Owning data high re-renders a wider subtree, so the extra layer costs render work unless children are memoised, and the wrapper is pure overhead where one component would do.
Duplicated or competing state: where a hook, ViewModel, Bloc or store already owns the data for the subtree, a container competing with it becomes a second model layer.
Dogmatic enforcement is a real cost: the split was widely imposed on codebases that did not need it, which is exactly what the original author's 2019 update retracted.

participants.responsibility: Renders the markup for the values it was handed and reports intent through the callbacks it was given; holds at most UI-local state (open, hover, active tab) and never loads or mutates the data it displays.

participants.role: Supply half (container, hook, state holder or action)
participants.responsibility: Obtains the data from its source, owns loading, error and empty handling, and renders or feeds the presentational component with values down and events up. It usually contains no markup beyond composition.

The declared interface between the halves - the values the view needs and the events it may raise; it is the only thing the presentational component knows, which is what makes it reusable across sources.
The store, API client, repository, service, session or template context the supply half reads; replaceable with a fixture or stub without touching the presentational component.
The place that decides which supply half feeds which presentational component - route, page, screen, or the test/story harness that renders the markup from literals.

use_cases: Design systems and component palaces: a library of markup-only components that any screen, story or visual test renders from literals.
One widget in several data contexts: a table, chart, card or form rendered from a live store in production and from fixtures in tests and demos.
Screens whose data source is being replaced (store to query library, REST to GraphQL, API to cache) while the markup stays untouched.
Teams where design and data work are separated: the presentational components are the designer-editable surface, the supply half the engineering surface.
Server-rendered pages: a controller action or view function assembles the data and a template or partial renders it from explicit locals only.
Visual-regression and accessibility testing: rendering every state of a component from props, with no backend and no mocking of the data layer.
Onboarding and review: a presentational component is the easiest artifact to hand to a newcomer because it renders from a literal and has no ambient dependencies.
React-Redux screens: connect or use selector-backed supply components to feed reusable views while keeping store subscriptions and dispatch wiring outside the render-only view.
Vue 3 components: props carry state into a child and declared emits send intent back to the parent, giving a presentational child an explicit contract.
Storybook stories: args provide literal component inputs and controls vary them interactively, making the presentational half testable without the application's data source.
avoid_when: A single component is the only consumer: keep the loading and the markup together, or extract a hook or state holder instead of adding a wrapper component.
The framework already separates logic from view without a second component (custom hooks, state hoisting, ViewModel, signals): use that idiom directly.
The markup genuinely needs the source - live subscriptions, virtualised windows, editors bound to a mutable model - because then the split only inserts a pass-through layer.
The markup is trivial (a styled box, a label): one component with local state is clearer than two, and the split pays only where reuse exists.
The team will not maintain the convention: without naming rules, lint enforcement and review, container sprawl or leaky children are the default outcome.
anti_patterns: Container sprawl: one wrapper per field or per source until the screen is mostly plumbing and the markup becomes untestable glue.
Presentational in name only: the 'dumb' component still reads a store, a global or an API client because it was convenient at the call site.
Prop forwarding through intermediates: values relayed through components that never read them, which is the problem the pattern was supposed to remove.
Taking the retraction as licence for chaos: rendering components that fetch inside their own render path, or data access duplicated in every leaf, because the container idea was declared unnecessary.
Two components for every trivial box: applying the split dogmatically rather than where reuse, testing or design independence actually pay.
A container competing with an existing state holder (hook, ViewModel, store), so the same data has two owners that can disagree.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: how it looks and where the data comes from are different responsibilities with different rates of change.
Dependency inversion: the presentational component depends on its input contract, not on a concrete store, service or API.
Single responsibility: data access, side effects and failure handling on one side; rendering and UI-local state on the other.
Open/closed principle: new data sources arrive as new supply halves around unchanged markup.
Unidirectional data flow: values down, events up - the view never writes what it was given.
Pure rendering: the same input should produce the same markup, which is the property that makes a component renderable from a literal and safe to inspect in isolation.
best_practices: Give the presentational component exactly the values it renders and the callbacks it raises - no data-source imports, no ambient lookups, no service locators.

Make the roles legible and enforced: name and place them consistently (components/ against containers/, view against hook or ViewModel) and back the convention with lint rules or review where the team depends on it.

Put the supply half where the ecosystem already keeps state - a custom hook, hoisted state, a ViewModel, a signal owner - and keep a wrapper component only where the source must be injectable per screen.
Handle loading, error and empty states in the supply half, so the view is never asked to represent a state it cannot know about.
Render the presentational component from a literal in tests and stories; needing a mock of the data layer is evidence that the view leaked.
Keep UI-local state (open, hover, draft text) in the view, and reserve the supply half for data and shared state.
Revisit the boundary when it hurts: the split is a tool, not an obligation - the original article's own update warns against enforcing it without necessity.
